4	
5	1. **Never put content behind a composition.** Removing a composition permanently deletes its content on every document that used it — no recovery through revisions. # Umbraco Rules

Project conventions, enforced by code in `Umbraco.Bench.Umbraco` where possible. The short version of the ten UmbraCommandments.

1. **Never put content behind a composition.** Removing a composition permanently deletes its content on every document that used it — no recovery through revisions. Compositions are for meta, settings, CTAs. Litmus test: *if we remove this composition later, is what remains still viable content?*
2. **There are six kinds of document type — file each in its folder.** Page (renders), Block (renders; lives in block list/grid; never used as a composition), Composition (composed onto others; never rendered, never pickable), Data (element; never renders — settings, events, people), Repository (container node; never renders), Repository Item (the pickable records inside a Repository).
3. **Data types never sit at the root of the data type tree.** Built-ins under `/Umbraco/<editor>`, custom ones under `/Custom/<editor>`. `DataTypeSavedHandler` enforces this on every save.
4. **Register in an `IComposer`, not Program.cs.** If `IUmbracoBuilder` can do it, it belongs in `Composers/`. Non-Umbraco concerns (CORS, App Insights) go in `WebApplicationBuilder` extension methods.
5. **Production runs in production mode.** Umbraco Application Url set, `--configuration Release`, HTTPS only, no model generation, no template editing. `appsettings.json` ships configured this way — don't soften it; put dev conveniences in `appsettings.Development.json`.
6. **Aliases are English and camelCase.** No exceptions.
7. **Dictionary keys are PascalCase with dots** (`My.Dictionary.Item`), and a dictionary folder never has values of its own.
8. **Media always lives in a folder.**
9. **The content root only holds Repositories.** The site hangs under the WWW `siteRoot` node; going multi-site means adding another Page beneath it, not re-architecting. Because WWW never renders, the site Page needs a **domain** or nothing answers on `/` — assign `/` for a single site, a hostname each for several.
10. **uSync everything — commit `Umbraco.Bench.Umbraco/uSync/`.** Export is automatic; you should not need to trigger it. On Umbraco Cloud, use Umbraco Deploy instead.

Two posts about why MCP is awesome. Let me draft: **Post 1: "Why MCP is awesome: tools that actually fit the job"** Rich text block 1: "

The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is the reason this very site exists. Not a theme, not a plugin — a whole content model, pages, images and all, assembled by an agent talking to Umbraco over MCP. Before MCP, an assistant could only talk; with MCP, it can do: create document types, publish pages, upload media, assign domains. The tools are not bolted on afterwards — they are the interface.

What makes MCP elegant is that the same protocol works everywhere. The Umbraco MCP server exposes the CMS's own management API as tools; an editor MCP server does the same for content. One agent, two servers, zero custom glue code. The model never scrapes a backoffice or guesses at an endpoint — it calls a named tool with typed arguments and gets structured results back.

" Image block: network-lines-dots, caption: "A network of lines and dots — every MCP tool is a node the model can reach. Photo: Conny Schneider on Unsplash." Rich text block 2: "

There is a quiet benefit to tool-driven work: every step is verifiable. Each call returns a real id, and each id can be read back. When a schema write lands, you fetch the document type and confirm the properties; when a page is created, you fetch the page and check the values. Nothing is taken on faith, and nothing fails quietly — a bad payload comes back as an error that says exactly what to fix.

It also keeps the architecture honest. Because the agent must go through Umbraco's own APIs, the conventions of the platform — document type folders, compositions, block grids — are enforced by the CMS itself rather than by prompt instructions. The result is a site that looks exactly like one built by hand in the backoffice, because in every way that matters, it was.

" Quote block: quote: "MCP turns 'please update the site' from a hope into a workflow: named tools, typed arguments, verifiable results." attribution: "— the whole reason this blog exists" **Post 2: "Why MCP is awesome: one protocol, every model"** Rich text block 1: "

MCP's superpower is not any single tool but the protocol itself: one standard way for models to discover and call capabilities, implemented by every major client and server. Write a tool server once and it lights up in Claude, in editors, in CI agents — anywhere that speaks MCP. The blog you are reading was assembled by exactly such a client, driving two MCP servers against a local Umbraco instance.

For a content platform this is a big deal. Umbraco ships a management API; the MCP server wraps it as tools; the agent composes them into a site. Schema first, then content, then a domain, then a published page — each step a tool call, each result a confirmation. The same calls a human would make in the backoffice, minus the clicking.

" Image block: code-on-screen, caption: "Colourful source code on a screen — the raw material of every tool call. Photo: Chris Ried on Unsplash." Rich text block 2: "

There is also something quietly awesome about building a site this way: the content model and the content are created in one continuous conversation. The document types that shape the blog exist moments before the posts that use them, and the generated models that the Razor views compile against appear as soon as the schema is saved. Model, content, code — one loop, no context switching, no 'export the schema and paste it somewhere' dance.

If you have ever wanted your CMS to feel less like a place you visit and more like a place you talk to, MCP is the bridge. This blog is the proof: two posts, a front page, five photos, a domain on / — all of it through the protocol.

Also — hmm, one consideration: the front page will get the domain "/". Its node name "Blog" — with a domain assigned, the URL is "/" regardless of name. Good. Let me create the front page now.

The Model Context Protocol turns a chat assistant into something that can actually do the work — here is what that feels like when you build a whole site through it.

The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is the reason this very site exists. Not a theme, not a plugin — a whole content model, pages, images and all, assembled by an agent talking to Umbraco over MCP. Before MCP, an assistant could only talk; with MCP it can do: create document types, publish pages, upload media, assign domains. The tools are not bolted on afterwards — they are the interface.

What makes MCP elegant is that one protocol works everywhere. The Umbraco MCP server exposes the CMS's own management API as tools; an editor MCP server does the same for content. One agent, two servers, zero custom glue code. The model never scrapes a backoffice or guesses at an endpoint — it calls a named tool with typed arguments and gets structured results back.

There is a quiet benefit to tool-driven work: every step is verifiable. Each call returns a real id, and each id can be read back. When a schema write lands, you fetch the document type and confirm the properties; when a page is created, you fetch the page and check the values. Nothing is taken on faith, and nothing fails quietly — a bad payload comes back as an error that says exactly what to fix.

It also keeps the architecture honest. Because the agent must go through Umbraco's own APIs, the conventions of the platform — document type folders, compositions, block grids — are enforced by the CMS itself rather than by prompt instructions. The result is a site that looks exactly like one built by hand in the backoffice, because in every way that matters, it was.

content.text:
Everything is done and verified. The site is live and Umbraco is still running in the background.

## Report

**What was built** — a complete blog site in Umbraco.Bench, built entirely through the two MCP servers:

- **Schema** (`umbraco`): three block element types (`richTextBlock`, `imageBlock`, `quoteBlock`) filed in the Blocks folder; a `Blog Block Grid` BlockGrid data type (12 columns, all three blocks, verified by read-back); `blogFrontPage` and `blogPost` document types in the Pages folder with templates assigned; `siteRoot` → allows `blogFrontPage` → allows `blogPost`.
- **Media**: a `Blog` folder with 5 Unsplash photos imported (4 used, credits in the image captions).
- **Content** (`umbraco-editor`): a `Blog` front page under WWW with title, intro and one rich-text block; two published posts — *"Why MCP is awesome: tools that actually fit the job"* (1 Oct 2026) and *"Why MCP is awesome: one protocol, every model"* (8 Oct 2026) — each with publish date, excerpt, listing image, and a 4-block body (rich text → image → rich text → quote).
- **Domain**: `/` (en-US) assigned to the front page, not WWW.
- **Rendering** (per AGENTS.md, no custom renderers): pages use `@await Html.GetBlockGridHtmlAsync(Model, "body")`; one adapter per block in `Views/Partials/blockgrid/Components/<alias>.cshtml` maps `BlockGridItem<T>` to plain models in `Models/Blocks/` (`RichTextModel`, `ImageModel`, `QuoteModel`); one ViewComponent per block (`Components/`) renders `Views/Shared/Components/<Name>/Default.cshtml`. Tailwind classes in the views; `npm run build` produced `wwwroot/dist/site.css` + `main.js`.
- **uSync** exported everything automatically (content types, data type, templates, content, media).

**How to view it**: Umbraco is running — open **https://localhost:44317/** for the front page (post list with images, dates, excerpts). Posts at `/why-mcp-is-awesome-tools-that-actually-fit-the-job/` and `/why-mcp-is-awesome-one-protocol-every-model/`. Backoffice: `/umbraco` (admin@example.com / 1234567890).

**Verified by curl**: all three pages return **200**; the front page shows its block + both posts; each post shows all 4 blocks (2 rich-text, 1 figure with signed image, 1 blockquote); rich text renders as real HTML (`@Html.Raw`, no escaped `<p>` anywhere); zero "Could not render component"; a signed image URL returns 200; `dotnet build` passes with 0 errors.

**Notes / workarounds** (nothing is broken):
- My first `dotnet run --no-launch-profile` booted on the default port 5000 in Production mode — I stopped it and restarted with `ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT=Development` + `ASPNETCORE_URLS=https://localhost:44317`, which is what `.mcp.json` expects.
- `publish-page`/`save-and-publish` with `includeDescendants: true` return "cancelled" (the bulk confirmation elicitation can't be answered here); publishing the front page first, then each post individually, works.
- One image (`laptop-desk-code.jpg`) is imported but unused — spare.
- The project is not a git repository, so nothing was committed; the uSync exports under `Umbraco.Bench.Umbraco/uSync/` are the schema source of truth to commit when you init git.
